utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Are the interpreters ready? Good morning. I hope everyone had a nice weekend and we can begin our work; I think, Mr. Prosecutor, with a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. The next witness we wish to call is witness number 1 on your witness list. This witness has sought the use of a pseudonym for his name, which is "Witness F". He has also asked for the image of his face to not appear and for the image to be distorted. I make that application and I have discussed it with Mr. Mikulicic. I do not understand there to be any objection to the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic? Can the necessary measures be taken, please? Have they already been taken? Thank you. In that case, please have the witness brought in. We have to pull down the curtains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the declaration that the Registrar is going to give to you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated and answer the questions that the Prosecutor is going to address to you, please. WITNESS F

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of your evidence, you will be referred to by the name "Witness F". I would ask you that you not divulge your name or your current or past address during the course of your testimony. Would you, please, look at the sheet of paper that I am now going to show you and if your name appears on that paper, would you answer "yes" or "no", but do not say the name, just tell me "yes" or "no". Could it then be shown to Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit in order, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What is the number, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we see, please? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness F, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to take you back, if I can, to mid to late January of 1993, and ask if you could tell us where you were at about that time and what happened, particularly about the 21st and 22nd January 1993. Can you recall that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you at that time? Do not give me a specific address but you can name the town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was happening in Busovaca around that time, around 21st and 22nd January? Can you describe the events that were occurring then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th/20th January of 1993, these were unbearable days for all of us. Movement was limited, the right to gather, in particular. Not more than two or three men could be seen together. If a fourth was there, we would immediately be forced to separate in one way or another. In the evening of the 19th, as well as the 20th and the night between the 20th and the 21st, these were among the worst nights because ugly things were happening; explosions, devices were planted on almost all shops, stores, held by Muslims and they were quite numerous. There were about 50 such shops in the centre of town, so that on the 19th, two or three explosions destroyed two cafes and, on 20th January, it was a relatively peaceful day. In the evening of the 20th, again things became nasty and this could be felt first by the cutting of telephone lines and we knew straight away that something was about to happen. The same applied to my own home. First my telephone was cut, about 7.00 pm in the evening on 20th January and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there for a moment. I just want to ask you: these restrictive measures, you spoke of the fact that the right to gather was prohibited and that people were attacking premises, shop premises in particular. Who were these measures directed against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against us, the Muslim inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was directing the measures, who was responsible for imposing these restrictions on the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO police, headed by Dario Kordic and the actual perpetrators, Anto Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And from your answer, you are, yourself, Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the destruction of Muslim property, the shops, in Busovaca; do you know who was responsible for that, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone knows that because not a single Muslim could move around freely, especially not in the evening. The only people to move around were HVO policemen and HVO fighters, combatants, so they were the only ones who could have done it, no-one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this particular point in time -- that is 20th January, around 20th January 1993 -- were you civilian or were you in the military, in terms of your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that your house, on the 20th, the telephone was cut off, then you were going to go on to describe events following that and I interrupted you. Could you continue on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I expected or, at least I think I expected, that something was to happen and my expectations came true. I was with my family, my wife and children in our living room. We were watching television. About 10.15 in the evening, I heard footsteps on the balcony of my house and the next moment a strong explosion was heard to the right of my house. A window face is there, a window about 120 by 140 centimetres and it was totally shattered, the glass scattered on the living room floor. With my children and wife, I tried to escape, to go out through the back door of my house, because there is a door at the back, and that very moment, strong blows could be heard. The breaking of the front door and cries, "open, it is the HVO police". I asked, "what do you mean the HVO police?", the next answer came the same: "The HVO police". Fire broke out. They started shooting from the veranda through the living room, but I managed with my wife and children to escape through the back into the woods and to spend the night there. Throughout the night, until about 4.00 am, maybe even 4.30 in the morning, they were looting things, they drove off anything they thought could come in handy. When I say, "everything", they took away everything, so that nothing remained, including my own passenger car, all the household appliances, virtually everything. The next day, when I went to the house after all, I could not find even some underwear for my children. Everything was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see the people -- were you able to identify the people who were doing this looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just saw that they were wearing camouflage uniforms, and, according to their cries, that is that they were the HVO police, I could conclude who they were. According to what I saw from the dark, because after all I was only some 30 metres from the house, they switched on all the lights and I counted seven of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after this had happened to you, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This happened. Then about 8.00 in the morning, I went to the house. I checked, looking around for some things, my wife and I were looking for anything, either for the children or ourselves because, in fact, we had spent the whole night half dressed. This was the month of January, 20th to the 21st and it was cold, but we did not find anything. So I sent my wife and children in the direction of Kacuni and I moved to my brother's house who lived in town. That is where I stayed for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the next thing that happened after you had separated from your wife and you moved to your brother's house? What is the next significant event to happen after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st January, it was relatively peaceful. People behaved as if nothing had happened during the night, the same applied to the 22nd and the 23rd. Then, on the 24th, in the evening, a Saturday, again somewhere after 9.00 pm and until 5.00 or rather 4.00 am, explosions were resounding so that that night my shop was blown up, among others. My free shop -- tax free shop. I could see that because it was not far from where I was staying. One can see the centre of town where I had a shop. Maybe an hour or hour and a half later, things became quiet again and I think somewhere around 6.00 in the morning, the siren -- the fire brigade siren could be heard announcing danger. The next moment, while the siren was still ringing, shooting started and whoever happened, by chance, to be in the street, he was hit either with a sniper rifle or an ordinary rifle. In any event, one could not move any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going back for a moment, if I may, during that night, were you able to see your house from your brother's house, where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: house was on fire". Since only some 200 metres away there was small hill from which my house could be seen, the logical conclusion was that it was only my house that was burning and that was, in fact, the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I interpreted you again. You were talking now of the next day, 25th January, at 6.00 am when you heard sirens and then there was a shooting with a sniper rifle at people who happened to be in the streets. Tell us what happened when these circumstances developed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This lasted from 6.00 am until 3.00 pm. There was constant rifle fire, sniper shots, shelling, only of this part of town. So that it was unbearable. One just could not stay there. People panicked. A couple were wounded, a couple were killed and virtually the entire population was swept by panic. This was only natural because the HVO soldiers were approaching from all sides and especially from the upper part, which is a wooded area. They were getting closer and closer to this part, so that in front of them were already people who were fleeing towards the centre and the panic was immense, it was something quite horrifying. About 3.30, all of us were rounded up and upon our cries and pleas and the showing of white sheets and flags, begging them to stop shooting, that we were not resisting, that we would withdraw wherever they say, so that finally, they accepted this and when we reached the actual town square, there was some more shooting, as intimidation, and some mistreatment. There were, in my estimate, somewhere around 90 human beings, I can put it that way. Women and a few children were separated and returned home, whereas the rest of us, some 70 of us, were loaded on to buses, that is the proper word. The bus was already waiting and ready and it drove us to Kaonik, to the barracks of the former Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I am not clear which town he is talking about. Which town is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before I ask that question, might we call for redaction on page 9, line 5? The town that you were in where you were gathered together, driven to -- collected in the centre of where you started your journey to Kaonik, what was that town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said 60 or 70 people were loaded on to the bus; what was the sex of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was their age group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Age group, 90 per cent we were between 25 and 40 and the rest were maybe 55 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the youngest age of the men, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two or three boys of 14, 15 and 16 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the people who were put in this bus and taken to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to Kaonik -- I am sorry, who was it that took you to Kaonik? Who took you to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not clear. Could you, please, clarify for me? Who was responsible? Dario Kordic was responsible for everything, without a doubt, but you probably think of who was driving the bus and who was the escorts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The driver of the bus was called Zeljko Vareskovic Bubreg and there was a soldier escorting the bus whom I personally did not know because at that time there were a lot of soldiers there whom I did not know and then there were a lot of those who I did know. They were wearing the HVO insignia and I knew them personally, but there were soldiers there who wore the HV insignia and the Runolist Brigade. They had separate accents, they were not locals, from Busovaca. I believe they were from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Runolist Brigade, do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know. I saw that for the first time on that occasion and I was only able to read this Runolist Brigade and it had this flower that looked like edelweiss and they spoke a different accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Let the witness be shown Exhibit P17, please. Witness F, I would like you to look at the exhibit you are going to be shown. I would ask that it be displayed on the projection machine that is there beside you. I am wondering if you could tell me whether you could identify the objects shown on this exhibit when you see them. If you can identify them, whether you can explain to us what it is you are identifying. (Handed). Perhaps deal with them by the numbers, number 1 and number 2. Tell us what number 1 is and what number 2 is, if you would be so kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 means Croatian army and number 2 means Croatian Defence Council. Number 1 is Croatian army. Those were obviously foreigners, that is people who were not from our region and those wearing the HVO insignia were all our local people from the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just to -- I think you have said this, but I will just get you to repeat it; did you see soldiers wearing both of these insignia on that particular day; namely, 25th January 1993, in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Kaonik camp, what happened then? Firstly, what time did you get there, then what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because this was about five kilometres away from Busovaca, it took us about 10 minutes to get there, which, in my opinion, happened around 4.00 in the afternoon. We were unloaded, we were taken to the hangar, which is almost at the far end of this complex, this compound of the former JNA barracks. We were all lined up against a wall which was about seven or eight metres long and 25 metres wide, this hangar was. We arrived there and we found a group there, already staying there. So we covered about three walls, we were all made to face the wall. At that moment we heard that something was going on and we were ordered to turn around. When we turned around, in the middle of the hangar, a man was standing, a man whom I did not know, whom I had not seen before, and who literally said the following: "I am Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. Do not fear. You will not miss a hair from your head". I am a bit of a joker, even when I am in a bad place, so I said: "Sir, I am aware of the fact that I will not miss a hair from my head since I do not have any, what about my head?". He just sort of made a sign and did not respond. We spent the entire night there. There was nothing there, there was just concrete floor. It was insufferably cold. At one point a few soldiers came in and they took out several young men. It was more to take away their valuables, whatever they had on them, jewellery or money. We spent that night in the hangar, without anything. It was only in the morning that they provided us with several pallets. Those were the loading pallets for loading merchandise. So, a few people were lucky enough to be able to sit on it because there were not enough of those. We were also given a blanket per three or four persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you said -- you spoke of the fact that this person came in and said he was Zlatko Aleksovski and spoke to you. When you said he made a sign, what did he do when you said that you knew nothing would happen to the hairs on your head? Can you just describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gesture of waving off his head, meant, "may God help you", and in my view, and based on what happened later, that is what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The people that were in the hangar who were being lined up against the wall, did you know any of these people or did you know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew each other for the most part because about 80 per cent of us were from the downtown area and 20 per cent were those who were brought from the surrounding villages or from the wider urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that -- I think you said that apart from your group, that is the 60 or 70 that came by the bus, that when you arrived there, there was other people there as well. Did you know these other people or know of them, or know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were brought there and when we entered the hangar, we knew that we were not the first ones there. Obviously I knew most of them, 99 per cent of the people I knew, and if I did not know them, they knew me, so we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From your best recollection, are you able to say what their ethnic background was, these people that were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers at the camp when you arrived there, or anyone dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were only two or three young men who had parts of the camouflage uniform, either the trousers or the jackets, but there were just a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these, so far as you could ascertain, guards of the camp or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, they were all soldiers -- a guard was a soldier too. He also had the insignia belonging to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was anything taken from you or any of the other prisoners that were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing was taken away from me in the hangar. However, a bag full of money was taken away because they were entering in there without any control. Any one of the soldiers could come in and would be able to search you, do whatever he wanted and so, in that manner, they took away quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you had been there for a day or so, did you see anything happen to any of the prisoners that were kept in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these groups of soldiers who would come in, in order to either get the money or something, they would take out two or three men and they would come back with little blue marks or something, so they were roughed up a little bit but that was nothing in comparison to what was to happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to that, did you ever see a group of prisoners taken out of the room by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 26th in the morning, after that night spent in the hangar, one of the guards came with a piece of paper on which there were 15 names. He called out these 15 names and, as he was calling them out, we had to come to step out. Then outside in front of the hangar, ahead of this plateau, we were tied up, one tied up to another with a rope. I was number 14 in that line. However, fortunately for me, they must have used -- they used up the rope, so myself and another person, who was a relative of mine, remained untied. The 13 men were taken away to be human shields because they told us that this they were going to do immediately. In fact, Zoran Pusic said this to us. He was in charge there. The person who was tying people up was Zeljko, called Bubreg, and another man whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will hand you a piece of paper and I want you to write a name on it, if you would be so kind, for me. (Handed). Was one of the persons taken away to be used as a human shield, in fact, your brother? Once you have written that down, perhaps you could show it to me. (Handed). That person is your brother, the person whose name appears here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be shown to Mr. Mikulicic, if you would. (Handed). I tender that under seal, your Honours, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What is the registration number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that these 13 men were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How is it that you knew that they were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As they were being tied up, Pusic, who was a policeman, said: "You are going to be human shield in the village of Strane", so that we knew what was going to happen. Upon their return, of course, I talked to my brother and to the rest of them, so they described how it was, where they were and the fact that they were used as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did your brother tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did he tell me? That it was terrible. That they took them down below the village; that the soldiers stood behind them, about 20 metres behind them, with their weapons ready and they forced them to walk towards the village in a parallel line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you who it was that forced them to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did he say did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man Pusic took them there and below the village the other soldiers waited and he recognised his best man, the person who was his best man. When he looked at him, this man turned his head away. I can say who this person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do not use his name. Now, after spending some time in the warehouse, did you stay there all the time or were you moved somewhere else in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we spent that day there. Then they used them as human shields one more time, so we spent the day and the night there, then the next morning they were used as human shields one more time. The same 15 names were called out again because these were all men from downtown Busovaca and they were taken to the village of Merdani. Again, I was not there because, again, I was number 14 and only the 13 were taken -- as the 13 were being tied up, and I was waiting to be tied up too, Zeljko Vareskovic, who I knew very well, he said: "It is all right, no more are needed." They agreed to that so that only 13 men were taken to Strane. My brother said this and we actually knew right away -- I mean, we knew this independently. They spent 24 hours there. From their stories it was worse than the first time around. They took them to the rail road bridge where the -- it was a disused rail road bridge. The bridge was still there, but it was not used. They brought them there. They were tied up. They made them lean over the railing. They put barrels of their guns to their heads and they told them that if they did not obey, they that would all be shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you spent some time in the hangar, were you then moved somewhere else in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To where were you moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they returned, this group which went out for the second time. I think it was in the evening, when they moved us to the cells, to the prison. This was already a prepared structure. This much closer to the entrance to the barracks. There were two buildings there, so in one of them there were cells and that is where we were put. These cells measured three by three, that was all. We were 25 to 30 in there. They had half a metre of free space so that the doors could open and the rest was sort of raised by about half a metre by some boards, so that we could lie down. Imagine 25 to 30 people in a cell which measured three by three. These were sort of classic cells with iron doors, classic prison cells with small openings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When this 25 to 30 people who were crammed into the one cell, where did they sleep, what provision was made for their sleeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were only a few blankets in these cells, on those boards, so you could not sleep. If five or ten people would sleep, the rest would sit. Those of us who were beaten up, we could not sleep, so we sat around and we would let these people who had already started to do forced labour to get some rest, and some of them had their ribs broken too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the first night you were in the prison, did anything happen to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I experienced different things from the very moment I got in there. Let us say right after dark, maybe half an hour later, I would be brought out in the hallway and I would be beaten up. This would happen every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who brought you out into the hallway, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought out mostly by one person into this hallway. He must have received some instructions. He had my description because he knew exactly who I was. So he would simply bring me out of the cell. The cell door would not even close and I would already being beaten, but I was kicking and beating me and I would get bloody. At one point I had a wedding ring on my hand and he tried to take it off. I somehow managed to do it myself. It did not change anything, he kept coming back every night and beating me. Unfortunately, with the permission of the guards who stood by silently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, he beat me with his hands and kicked me. He did not use any other instruments, kicked and beat me with his hands. He was larger than I am, he was stronger than I am. He was strong and so he was able to beat me up badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he was kicking you, what position were you in? Were you standing or lying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, of course, I was standing, but after the first, second blow, I was, for the most part on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently come to find out what his name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually I do not know his name. But I do know that his surname was Marelja, that he came from Herzegovina. I could tell by his accent that he came from the region of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About how old was this man, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was about 25 to 30 years old. He was 180 or 185 centimetres tall. He weighed about 100 kilogrammes. He was very strong. He wore a beret and he limped in one leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the colour of his hair, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was blond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every night. Only two nights when I was trench digging, he did not. I thought myself lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where, precisely, did these beatings take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately in front of the cell, right there, just outside the door of the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from you, was anyone else there at any stage, that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were a couple of metres away, but they did not react at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned that, apart from two occasions, you were beaten every night. On those two occasions you were taken trench digging. Can you describe the circumstances of how it was you came to be taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, but there is something else that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you should tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third day after I was detained in the cell, I was selected and another guy and we were taken to the building at the entrance itself, the entrance to the camp or the barracks, which had one storey, and we were taken for some sort of informative interview, at least that is what we were told. A young soldier, one could almost call him a child, one could not really call him a serious soldier, he took us to this entrance to the camp. We were immediately shut up in a cell, which had rails and door and window, there were no glass panes, just the railing. The man was taken away. I stayed behind. Sitting on a military bed, 10 or 15 minutes later, this young man was brought back. In the meantime some strange things were happening, or rather they could not be called strange, they were normal. Fighters would come by and as 90 per cent of them knew me, they would call out: "So what, you got the wrong nation. No, you are not the wrung nation, you are unfortunately just in the form of humans". 15 minutes later this young man was brought back after being beaten up, then I was taken. I was taken upstairs and there is a room, a somewhat larger room, and in the middle of the room was a table, a ping pong table. When I entered through the door, there were two chairs at this table, one on each side, and a third on the third side. Three guys were standing against three windows with their backs stand -- they were looking outwards so I could not see who they were. At the table two men were sitting, two fighters, soldiers whom I knew personally very well. In fact, I was glad to see them. However, I would shortly be disappointed. They offered me cigarettes and coffee and I accepted and then some sort of a conversation started. But let me add that on this table there were six or seven various types of stakes, wooden, rubber, steel, even police truncheons. I was on a chair at one end of the table and after this cigarette and that coffee, the questioning started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just -- the two people that you recognised, do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I said that I was glad to see them, because we were many times together in the cafe next to my shop, even in my shop we had many a cup of coffee together. One of them is Katava Zeljko, an electrician by trade. The other is Zarko Petrovic, known as Tadija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was their nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say they started to ask you some questions. What questions were they asking you? What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the first questions asked was: why I had been in the house of my brother. I really did not have an answer to this question, but anyway, whatever I would have said, it would not have made any difference. They asked me questions about all kinds of things, even about certain Croats, who would socialise with us. After each question, after each answer, the three men who were standing behind my back would hit at me with whatever they could get hold of. Perhaps the easiest to bear were their kicks with their boots. This lasted three and a half hours. There was some terrible moments. At one point in time Marelja walked in. The man who had beat me every night. He hit me with his fist in the face, so he fractured my jaw, upon which I think it was Tadija, or actually Petrovic, jumped up and swore at him and said: "I told you, not the head".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did -- apart from these batons and sticks and things you described, did anyone have any other weapons which they threatened you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps after about three hours of this torture, one of these men pushed my head back and put a knife against my throat. I tried to press my neck against that knife. I did not care any more. I was at the end of my tether, but I did not succeed because again the reaction was: "I told you, not the head", this was said by Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you try to thrust yourself upon the knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But he was holding me so tightly that I did not manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had been beaten for approximately three hours in this place, what happened to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, they took me back to the cell, the same cell which had only iron rods as walls. I spent about half an hour there. It was very cold. I think I could not sit, I was simply jumping up and down from the cold. Then I was taken back to the cell, but a separate cell, number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say taken back to the cell, this is the cell block where you were taken out of originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just stopping there for a moment, would you look, please, at the plan that -- the overhead photograph that I will now show you? Your Honours, this is the same photograph that has been tendered in a number of occasions. I will make this one a new exhibit. I will ask the witness if you would for me, please, Witness F, to mark certain places for me on the photograph. (Handed). There is a copy for your Honours and one for the Defence. Witness F, I would like to put this on the overhead projector. You will need to actually mark the exhibit on the overhead projector because it will not appear if you just point to the screen. I want to take you back to start with, if I can. You should have in your hand a pen, a felt pen, which I will ask the usher to kindly provide you with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there are a number of places I would like you to mark for me. Firstly, when you said you arrived at the camp, that is when you arrived from Busovaca on 25th January, you were placed in a hangar in the camp. Are you able to point to that place, as best you can recall? I would ask you to write the number "1" at that spot, if you are able to locate the place? Can you point to it for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps put a circle around that hangar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You then said that subsequently you were taken to proper cells, proper prison cells where you were beaten, just about on every night. Could you draw a circle around that particular building and mark it with the number "2"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have now just spoken of an incident where you were taken to another building, where you were taken upstairs, with the ping pong table, and beaten for a period of approximately three hours. Would you mark that place with a circle and the number "3"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you just pull the photograph down a little bit so we can see it on the screen. Thank you very much. I tender that, your Honours, as the next Prosecution number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Witness F, I would like you to look at a photograph, if I could, now, please. Perhaps that photograph could be numbered the next Prosecution number in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is exhibit number 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could that be placed on the overhead projector? Witness F, looking at the photograph, obviously of a building, which is now shown to you, do you recognise the photograph of that building, what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, of course. It is the building I was taken to. This is the building, the first that you come across as you enter the camp, the only one with an upstairs floor, and where the torture room, one could call it, was, the room with the table tennis table in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was the room you were beaten in for three hours and you just marked on the plan as number 3; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just looking at that particular photograph, do you recall where it was in the building that you were taken? Perhaps you might point to it with a pointer that is there on the table in front of you. You need to point on the screen, are you able to point to the room or the building where you are taken to. For the purposes of the record, the witness is pointing to the top storey of the building on the left-hand side of the building as you look at the photograph, where three windows appear on the top floor. I tender that exhibit, your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting, could I have the photograph please, also?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have a copy here. I am sorry. (Handed). What was the next thing to happen to you in the Kaonik camp after you were taken back to your cell, after this beating that lasted for three hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken back to a solitary cell where I spent a couple of hours, after which I was moved back to the cell in which I was originally. I spent the night there in a sitting position because I could not lean on anything, not to mention being able to sleep. So the first day was relatively peaceful. However, the next evening, about 8.00 pm, I was called out to join a group going for trench digging. As it was dark, it was very dark, because after all this was winter time and it was 8.00 in the evening as we walked out in front of the building where two lines of soldiers, a gauntlet, on either side of the path we had to go between them and as soon as we walked in, they all got their weapons, we had to bend down our heads. No-one was allowed to utter a word. In that way, we were taken towards Gavrine Kuce, or actually beyond Gavrine Kuce, near Putis, to dig trenches and we spent the whole night digging, and the next day until about noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who called you out? Who called you out of your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A guard called our names out. The guard called Marko Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this a regular guard at the camp who was there often or was it somebody that you had not seen or known before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period of time, he was a regular guard. They had their shift and he would come to take his shift every other night. He was a regular guard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers that were outside that you were to get their rifles and run through, were they regular guards of the camp or were they soldiers who came into the camp, as best you can ascertain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were soldiers who came there. They were not regular guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken trench digging, were you guarded when you were doing the trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Two or three of us digging, there were two guards who were five to ten metres away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these, as best you could ascertain, guards that had come from the prison or were they soldiers that were engaged in active duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not guards, they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they dressed in the full military uniform of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under full combat gear. They even had helmets on their head and HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken trench digging, did you ever hear rifle fire or fighting going on nearby where you were trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no fighting at all, but near us a group of some 15 soldiers went by. They went to the road leading to Putis, they set fire to 10 to 15 houses. There were a few shots then, but this had no effect on us. We were not sheltered in any way, we just had to go on digging. So it had no effect whether anyone was shooting or not. This lasted for about 15 minutes. A couple of houses went up in flames. These same soldiers went by again and we spent the rest of the night digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not the selection of people to go trench digging, did that appear to be organised systematically or was it just random, that you were able to ascertain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Everything was organised, to the last detail. Everything was done according to lists that were prepared in advance. The guards simply were given this piece of paper with the names on it of between 15 and 30, depending on the needs. The groups were not larger than 30. Then they would call out the names and that is the way it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think you said that you went trench digging on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The first time in the area between Gavrine Kuce and Putis. Maybe we were lucky because the guards were from Vitez, so that they did not mistreat us. They even gave us water and something to eat, perhaps the same food they had, so that the night passed in digging and no mistreatment. However, I was sent specially to Kula, which was already infamous because terrible things were happening there and whoever came back was beaten up, had broken bones and things and some individuals who had been digging there said, even my brother said that they were looking for me. And, indeed, they did send me to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was looking for you, as best you could ascertain from what your brother had told you? Who was it that was looking for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards who were there at Kula, they were looking for me because they had a piece of paper with my name on it, and they asked every group: "Who is so and so?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Among those guards I did not know anyone. When I got there, that very moment I was called out, separated and ordered to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is going to be a long incident, your Honour, and I notice that it is 11.30. Rather than have the witness start halfway through only to interrupt him, may we break at this moment? If your Honours wish to take a break, I assumed you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to have a 20-minute break, which means until 11.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness F, you were about to describe to us the circumstances surrounding an incident where you were taken out to do trench digging on a second occasion, to a place called Kula. I am wondering if you would pick up that incident and tell us what happened to you when you were taken out to this place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken out of our cells, loaded on to a truck and driven to Kula. As we got off the truck, we had to go in a single file, with our heads bowed for about a kilometre or two, where we were met by guards who stopped us and one of the guards, whom I did not know, read out my name. He had a piece of paper with my name on it and he told me to move out of line, which I did. He took me, just me, while the others stayed behind, and he took me to a very big oak tree, where there are lots of such trees, or rather a beech tree, about 60 to 70 centimetres in diameter. He ordered me to dig five centimetres from the tree trunk. This I found strange, that somebody should order me to dig there because normally you could not dig there anyway, but they were not interested in that, so I started digging, for about 10 minutes only, when one of those guards came for me again and took me 10 to 20 metres away from the group which had joined us in the meantime and, in this part there were some oak trees which are not very high but they have very thick trunks. He placed me behind this oak tree and ordered me to take off all my clothes. To my misfortune I had a watch on my hand, which I had simply forgotten to hide in the cell. Because we knew what was happening up there, so we had tried to conceal some things in our cells and I had forgotten to do that. This was the first thing he took from me. He ordered me to take off all my clothes. As I was rather well dressed for prison conditions, I had shoes on me, trousers, woollen trousers, what we called a McCleod sheepskin jacket, which they had not taken away from me throughout that time until then. Why, I do not know, because out of all the prisoners that there were, not one left with his own property, with his own clothes, not to mention jackets, windbreakers, trousers, shoes, all this was taken away. Anyway, he told me to undress and all I had left on was a slip. He took my jacket, my trousers, he searched all the pockets and as he did not find anything, he started becoming angry. He had in his hand a pickaxe handle which is quite thick and quite large, maybe one metre 20 long and five, six, seven centimetres in diameter. At one end, the other it can be up to eight centimetres wide. He ordered me to sing. I asked him, "for heavens sake, what do you want me to sing?". He said literally what I should sing: "I am", by name so and so, "a Mujehedin is fucking the Ustasha's mother". I found this difficult to do and since this guard was addressed as Nedeljkovic, so my conclusion was that he was Serb by nationality and the Nedeljkovic family, as far as I know, were from Dusina. I found it even more difficult to understand why he was forcing me to sing this. However, after his first blow, I did start to sing but very quietly, very softly. He said: "I told you loudly, so that it can ring in everyone's ears". I said that that was out of the question, upon which he hit me with all his might with that handle in the legs, so that for a moment I thought that my legs were gone. Again, after that blow, I had to sing and I sang rather more loudly. I suppose he was satisfied. His aim was for the others to hear that I was singing this, so that three of them within a minute or so would come up to me and start to hit me with whatever they had because I was cursing the Ustasha mother. Of course, this was hard to endure, but one can endure all kinds of things. Then they took me back to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to stop you for a moment. The person who beat you with the handle, you said you thought he may have been a Serb because of his name. What was he dressed in? How was he dressed? Can you describe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage. It was a camouflage uniform. He was a short man, maybe 160, 165 tall. He was dark haired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he had no insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand him to be a Serb soldier with the HVO or do you have some other explanation to why he may have been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the Serbs, persons of Serb ethnic background who remained in that area, had already been incorporated into the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you understood him to be part of HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the other soldiers that came up you and beat you also, did you understand them to be part of HVO or could you give them some other description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that they were considered to be part of the HVO but they really indeed were part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why is it that you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happened to you after this beating? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken back to dig trenches and I continued to dig. In fact, it was not real digging because it was impossible to dig in that place because of this very big thick routes, but I had to and I continued to do it the whole day. It was a very, very long day. There would be two or three minutes of rest, five minutes of beating and this continued throughout the day. Around 12.00 the three of them who kept coming every five to ten minutes, they would come by and they would hit me with something, with their boots, with their hands, with the shovels. For instance, if I bent to hit the ground, the soil with this pickaxe, he would come behind me and hit me. Then around 12.00, these three finally arrived together and sat near me. I had dug up about maybe 50 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who are these three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the three soldiers who had the insignia, whom I did not know but they kept beating me all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the three took a piece of newspaper and he rolled it up into some kind of a torch and set it -- and set it aflame and the other one came behind me and he started burning off my beard, which was about two or three centimetres long at that time, and then he did it on both sides. There was this crackling sound. It was as if you put water into hot oil, that is the noise that it was making. This went on for about 10 or 15 minutes, this singeing and their aim was to burn off my beard because, for some reason, it bothered them a lot. Out of this 30 men who were there with me, nobody dared say anything. One of them was about 10 metres from me and I heard him clearly, he said: "Do not come close to him, because he is not going to leave here alive". After this burning, maybe half an hour passed, I continued to dig. They did not give me any water. I asked for some, but it would have been better had I not because I got more blows over my back for it. Two of them then came back and they took off my hat from me, like this. (Indicating). I am demonstrating how they did it. They put it on a stick, on a piece of wood that was maybe 50/60 centimetres long and they set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sort of hat was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a beret like this. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is a kind of a felt, like standard berets. I am not an expert to tell you, but you can see it. This is what it was made of. So, it cannot burn this thing, it just turns into carbon and they kept it on the stick and when they managed to singe about 70 per cent of it, they gave it back to me, to my hands, and they ordered me to eat it. I never tasted anything as ugly as this. I was already very fatigued because of all the work, I had not had any water, but I had to eat this hat. I tried to get to a piece that was not singed, that was not burned, but I could not, it was hard. So I had to keep chewing. If I stalled or if I tried to get out of it, I would get a blow. I would get a kick or I would be hit by a handle of wood, so I had to do it. So, I chewed it and I ate, I think, 70 to 80 per cent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did it take you to eat that much of the hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No longer than one hour. Because they kept hurrying me, so it went on for one hour, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had been forced to do this, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left. Then five minutes later, they again came back, I repeat, they again came back because I never was left alone for more than five minutes during that day, somebody would come back. Then on that occasion they had me take off my shoes. They gave me some sneakers which had no soles any more. I do not know where they took the shoes, they took them with them. I received several blows with one of the handles and one of them said: "You are still in luck, but the night is coming, Mr.. Hosovac is coming and he will finish you off." We knew, myself and the others who used to work at Kula, we knew about this man, we knew that he was dangerous, and the night will come, Hosovac will come. He came over to me and said: "Take your shovel and take the pickaxe"; I said: "Why, for God's sake?". He said: "We need to fix something up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was he dressed, this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A black uniform with a black beret and a HOS insignia on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was different from what you have described as worn by the ordinary HVO soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know whether we got an answer to that question. I will ask the question again: this uniform was different from the uniform you described as being worn by the ordinary HVO soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It was completely black with black beret and a separate insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask you to look at this document I will now show you. If you recognise the document, can you describe what it is, please? Might it be placed on the overhead projector? (Handed). We will give it its number and then show it to Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the exhibit number 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at this document as it appears on your screen, Witness F, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. That is the insignia that this man wore on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, if your Honours please. I do not have a copy for your Honours at the moment but we will make one available in due course, to your Honours and to Mr. Mikulicic. Now, the gentleman dressed in the black uniform with this insignia, ordered you to gather your digging equipment and follow him, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He ordered me to take the pickaxe and the shovel and follow him. I asked him why. He said: "We are going up there to fix something, something was not done right". So he took me about 50 to 60 metres away from that clearing where we had worked towards the forest and when I entered -- when we entered the forest, just a couple of metres, he said, "stop". He said, "start digging". I said: "what am I supposed to be digging", because there was nothing there, there were no trenches, no fox holes, nothing. He said this: "you are not a fool, you know how to dig a hole and the hole is for you".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you understand this to mean, when he said, "the hole is for you"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That it was the end, that he was going to kill me, that there was no way out, that the end was there. But at that moment, I also started thinking he and I were there alone. I thought maybe I could escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand the hole to be your grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. That is exactly it. It could not have had any other meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I had a pretty good shovel, not too big, not too small, I saw that the end was there, so I thought to hit him with it and to run and see if I make it. However, he was a well-trained soldier, obviously, and he did not come anywhere close to me, so I started digging, but I started delaying it because if this was the last thing that I did, I was going to take my time. At one point, he approached me from the left-hand side and he took me by the lapel and he said: "Where is the money? Where is the gold?". I simply told him, "there is no money, there is no gold. Whatever I had was taken away. Whatever was left behind was burned. There is nothing left". He obviously had full information about my wealth and how much money I had, so when I told him that I did not have the money or gold, he tried -- in fact, he showed with his hand that he was about to hit me and he had a black glove with cut-off fingers and studs, so that a blow would hurt even more, so he made a fist and I said: "Man, what kind of a person are you?". He said: "Why?"; "if you want to hit me then do, but I think we can come to an agreement". To which he responded, and he said: "So what can we agree on?" I said: "It is not a problem, you know everything about me. I do not know you". He said, "that is correct". I tried to trick him into telling me his name, but I did not succeed. I said: "Tell me your name, this is going to finish, you will get something from it". However, he did not agree to that, so then I offered him: "You know who I am, you know that I am not bare", which in Bosnian means I still had some stuff stashed away. Then he said: "Oh, what do you have left?". I said: "I have two rings, each worth 1,000 German Marks. I have some cash in the cell, they can be yours". Then he offered me a cigarette. I turned him down because I had a pack of cigarettes in my pocket but I never dared ask. I did not dare even reach for my pocket, so I told him I had cigarettes, that I did not need them. Then he handed me a lighter and he took me with him. I stopped him at one point and I asked him: "very well, I promised you all this, what do you give me in return?". He said: "What do you want?". I told him: "Please protect me; protect me and these 30 men, at least tonight". Then he explicitly said that he was going to see to it. This was already 6.00 pm in the evening, at least that was my estimate because I did not have a watch. The shift which guarded us during the day was changing, were being replaced by another one and this new shift had already arrived so he approached one of the guards and said: "See this friend of mine, do not let anyone touch him tonight". His answer was: "Who cares". This HOS man said: "Guy, you are going to be dealing with me". To which he just shrugged and agreed with him. So, we went on for maybe 10 metres or so and there was another group of three guards. He approached them. I stayed behind at the edge of the forest. He went over to them and brought them over to me. I knew all three of them, even though they were not from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many men were in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ones who were digging? There were about 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The three of them approached me. One of the three asked me: "Do you know me?". My answer was: "Maybe". Because whatever you said it did not matter, you would be beaten either way. Whatever you said you would be beaten. If you, by some chance, did not address him with "sir" or the way he wanted, you would be beaten, so I did not know any more what to say, so I said: "Maybe I may have seen you somewhere, I do not know". His words were not to pretend to be a fool because we had so much business dealings that we knew each other well, because he made a lot of money off of the merchandise that he was buying from me. I think we smoked two or three cigarettes there and we had a conversation which was very, very different now, almost friendly. But after those three cigarettes, I was a bit dizzy and I said: "Please help me to go and dig along with the others because they are all digging and I am standing here". He said: "But why are they digging so hard there?". I said: "We have been working at this pace for the last 24 hours and without the any water or anything. So if you want to help us, give us some water". I am thankful to him to this day because then he went and brought us water so that we could quench our thirst. Especially myself, I was burning inside from having eaten the hat and all that. We continued to dig all the night but not as intensely as before. At one point he let us know that we should start digging harder because there was a commander coming from somewhere with two or three girls, so that we should dig harder so that he could see that we work harder. But it did not matter whether we worked harder or less hard because the first seven people about that were in the trench, as they were rising in order to throw out the dirt, the soil, he would hit them with a rifle butt or with something else. Then after that he was satisfied and he left. So, we spent that night digging, though not that intensely, and there was no abuse. In the morning, the next morning, we received breakfast for the first time. If we can call it that. We were 30. There were 25/26 maybe slices of bread and 10 canned fish portions. I think that there were 200 gramme portions. It was not cooked. But out of these 10 cans, three were empty. So this was distributed to us so we had 10 persons per can, but those three that were empty, meant that three groups were without that. The soldiers would come over to the ones who got the empty cans and say: "Did you have enough? Was there enough food?". They would say "yes", and they were beaten because they were lying. The next one said he did not have enough, then he was beaten because he had too much of an appetite. So, at least we had some bread and that took off the edge from our hunger. Then one of the soldiers who was beating and mistreating me all day the day before, took me aside. He had a sniper rifle with him. He took me into a dug-out and asked me, whose sniper rifle was this. I said I did not know that. He looked at me for a few minutes and said: "So, you do not, okay, very well. You can go". So we kept digging until about two o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then taken back to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First they shut us up in that village in a small room and we were locked up there for about half an hour waiting for transportation because they told us that we were free, that we would be taken to the cells. We felt we were being born again because to go back to the cell was like being born again, at least we knew what to expect there. We were locked up there for about half an hour when a new group arrived of about 17 new people, whereas the 30 of us got into the trucks and went back to the barracks to the prison, to the cells. When I got there, I looked around before entering the cell. We were allowed to wash our hands in a barrel, which we had used for those 15 days to pour water into the toilet. We also washed hands, we also washed our faces because there was no other water. We got very little water for drinking. I looked around and this HOS member was standing in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where are you at this stage? Tell us, when the HOS man was standing in the hall, where was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the left, to the left side of the corridor where the cells are, the cells 1, 2, 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are in the Kaonik prison now, by this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we were brought back to the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called my brother to bring me my purse, which was hidden with him and he brought it. I gave him the two golden rings, I gave him about 70 German Marks, 20, 30, 40,000 Croatian dinars, I cannot remember exactly. I gave him all this from the bottom of my heart, because after all he saved us that night, because the nights were the worst and the following night already would prove it from the group which took our place. As it was already dark, it was winter time and darkness falls early. I managed to reach cell number 11, which someone -- I do not know whether the prison commander -- anyway, this was part of his responsibility. This was a cell where people were put when they were spared physical labour. There were two Iranians and a couple of people from Busovaca who were also on some kind of sick leave and I was given two cubes of sugar, which meant a great deal. From one of the Iranians who was a doctor, I was given two pills and an ointment. He rubbed it in because I was as black as this jacket. Only my head was still white. I was given these two pills and I was massaged by him with this ointment. I managed to swallow something, though I had to use a straw to eat the last 10 days. I could not put a crumb of bread into my mouth it was so painful. I would eat a couple of mouthfuls and I swallowed these two pills. I lay down and I fell asleep from the effect of the pills. So that I slept that night. Somewhere around 5.00 am, a terrible noise was heard, cries, shouts, blows, beatings in the corridor. I was awakened too, but I was told to keep quiet, the people who were with me in the cell. As I did not care any more, and the first thing I thought was that they were going to slowly execute us one by one, because February 8th at 12.00, the exchange had been scheduled for 12.00 that day for all of us prisoners. So I thought they probably wanted to get rid of as many as us as possible before the exchange. As I had become accustomed to the beating, having been beaten so badly, I was the first to pluck up courage to knock on the door of the cell, requesting as a pretence to go to the toilet. The guard immediately opened the door and let me go. I headed towards the toilet, but I secretly looked around to see what was happening in the corridor. HV policemen, one of whom I know personally, were beating these men and this HOS man who had mistreated us at Kula. Later on I learned, because rumour spread quickly and we learned very shortly afterwards why this was happening. The reason was that when us 30 came down from Kula, 17 others replaced us and they worked for the rest of the day normally, but that very night -- we were all afraid of the nights, because they were roasting lambs, they drank a lot of alcohol, and then they would go out to the trenches, the front-lines where people were digging, and then they would beat up and massacre people. So on the night between the 7th and the 8th these 17 people were disastrously beaten up. Out of the 17, 15 returned; out of those 15, I knew each and every one of them, but you could not recognise them. They were so badly beaten up. Two guys did not return, they were killed at Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the places that you were taken trench digging. I want you to look at the map that he I now show you. Using the highlighting pen, would you please indicate on this the places that -- the two places that you were taken when you were trench digging -- maybe three places. The places you were taken for trench digging. (Handed). Again, if you could do that on the ELMO for me. When you mark them, if you highlight them, could you just tell us which place it is that you are highlighting and then we will put numbers again on the places. First, could you do that for us, please? Perhaps if you do it in order it would be helpful. I think you said you were taken to Putis on the first occasion, if I remember correctly. Do you see that place there, could you indicate where it was you were taken trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now put a circle around it. Mark it with the number "1", if you would. Now, the next place you were taken, were you taken to Strane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was all in the same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was during one night. We were working all night. You cover 10 kilometres easily. So that the area that I will now mark was roughly the area that we spent that night working in. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, that is fine. Now the next place that you mentioned was Kula. Again, if you could find that for me on the map. Indicate the place where you worked when you were at Kula.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you mark that with the number "2". Then the area where you were working on the trenches, are you able to indicate that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. I tender that, if your Honours please, and we will give it the next number in order. You said a moment ago in your evidence that you anticipated being exchanged on 8th February 1993. Why had you expected that you would be exchanged on that date, namely, 8th February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learned that at Kula from the soldiers, as a good piece of news that they conveyed to us by saying: "You are lucky after all, because you will be exchanged tomorrow at 12.00", which meant 8th February, that it had been arranged for that day. Since we had already been registered by the Red Cross, there were some early indications that this could happen on the 8th at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened on the 8th at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 8th February, the morning after that big hullabaloo with the Croatian police, who arrested its own soldiers and detained them, we were simply taken in front of the building, the building of the prison, so that we were all there, almost all of us in a group, already about eleven o'clock. None of us had watches, it may even have been ten o'clock in the morning when we were taken out. However, the exchange was delayed because of these two men who had been killed in the night between the 7th and the 8th because the Red Cross insisted on finding them too and they were not to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was present out the front when you were taken out there, do you recall anyone being present when the exchange was to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the exchange, there were quite a number of them. All the guards. Anto Sliskovic was present, Mr. Aleksovski was present, all of them were present. Even this friend of me, Petrovic Zarko, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the two men who had been killed, were you then all exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least as far as we knew, we thought that all of us had been exchanged, but some people did stay behind in the prison, the two Iranians, and all the others who were detained from the Busovaca area were exchanged and allowed to go whichever side they wanted. Some went to Busovaca, some to their own villages, some towards Zenica, it depended. However, there is something else that happened before we actually boarded the bus: some of the things that were found on this HOS man and the two soldiers who were beaten up by the HVO police on them some valuables were found. Among these three rings, some money, a couple of watches, obviously the things that were of value because the rest he had probably shared out. So that one of the guards brought these things and asked who they belonged to and gave these things back. By chance my two rings were there and another one ring only belonging to a Burbur, an old ring of value, so that is all that was returned, only three rings out of the jewellery. Then among the money there was only some 20 Marks that nobody wanted to take and also there were a couple of watches that nobody cared about any more, that is what was returned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing Mr. Aleksovski in the camp, had you known him before you went to Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him very often when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time when he introduced himself in the hangar. I saw him a second time when a young man was brought back from Kula with his ribs broken and when he asked him, "Mr. Governor, please help us", and he, indeed, did help him. He sent him a pill for dysentery. That is when I saw him. That was the second time. The third time, when he was standing in the corridor, and distributing papers to the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that you would recognise him again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say for sure because, in a sense, we were not really -- we did not really dare to look at him. He was short, as far as I remember. Maybe I would, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In a moment, you will be answering questions after those put to you by Mr. Niemann. I think that perhaps Mr. Mikulicic will do the cross-examination, perhaps it would be better to begin after the lunch break. So we are going to have a lunch break now. Have a good lunch all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Are the interpreters ready?
