utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Defence? I take advantage of this opportunity to greet Mr. Joka, who we have not seen for a long time, and Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Mr. F, I am Mr. Mikulicic, Defence counsel for the accused in this case. I am going to ask you some questions and I would like you to answer them as well as you recollect them. Mr. F, when you gave your statement, you said that you spent -- lived in Busovaca a long time. How long was this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From when -- from my birth until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During this period, you achieved a status there which can be described as being a wealthy member of the Busovaca community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you engaged in sports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not like to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase, you are absolutely right. Is it true that a lot of people knew you as a prominent athlete in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. F, on the day which you described when the conflict started in Busovaca, you said that you noticed some foreign soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not notice, I saw them. I personally saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what do you mean by "foreign soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had HV insignia on them and, "Runolist Brigade", or, "Edelweiss Brigade", was on their camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that they were speaking in a different accent. What kind of accent was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an accent from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where Herzegovina is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is part of which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is part of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. F, who brought you to Kaonik? I mean, which persons were these? The soldiers from Herzegovina, or were there some other soldiers who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a lot of military personnel there, a lot of uniformed men in the HVO -- with HVO insignia, HV insignia and Runolist Brigade insignia. They rounded us up on to 15 square metres in the main square and then they loaded us on these buses, and the driver who was driving us was a local man from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who received you in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first nobody received us. The bus simply came to a stop in front of the hangar, the entrance to the hangar. There were two guards, two soldiers to the side and while even still on the bus, we were ordered to file out one by one, enter there and face the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said "the guards", "soldiers"; were these guards from Kaonik or were these soldiers part of the group of soldiers who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not guards from Kaonik, but they were guards from Busovaca. For instance, one of them was from the village of Boselj. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So is it true that the two persons who you called guards were not guards at Kaonik, but among the soldiers who brought you up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please correct me then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers who were placing us on these buses in Busovaca, they remained there. Only one soldier went along together with the driver and the driver was armed too, so it was only the two of them who brought us to Kaonik and in Kaonik in front of the hangar, other soldiers were waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, the other soldiers who waited in front of the hangar at Kaonik were not guards at Kaonik? That is my question, really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How come they were not? They were there with weapons, they had to be guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Allow me to rephrase my question: the two men of whom you spoke, did you see these two later as guards, while you were in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day, the first night, the second day and the second night -- they were there non-stop, in front of the hangar on guard posts. Later we saw them in the cells too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What types of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any insignia there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. F, you described in your statement how you were taken out of Kaonik and taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who watched you while you dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time we went digging we were watched by the soldiers who were from Vitez. The second time people who -- I do not know the people, God knows where they came from, but there were a few of them from Busovaca whom I knew, but those never came even close to us, not even 10 to 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During the first or second digging, did you notice whether you were watched by any of the guards from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the front-line at Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had no time to think about it. I did not have the time to look around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. F, correct me if I am wrong, but tell me: did you not state that the first night when you arrived to the prison, and put in the cells, that you were taken out by a person called Marelja and he beat you up in front of the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this Marelja was not the a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was he, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a soldier, an HVO soldier, who was free to move wherever he wanted. He was free to enter, leave. He was free to enter the prison, the cells, whatever he wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was a detainee in this prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that and I do not believe he was. In fact, he was not there for sure, he was not a detainee there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. F, you said that from the building with the cells, you were taken to another building. Do you know who was placed in -- who was placed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the so-called intervention platoon or the special purpose platoon, that was the first building next to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of this intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Kaonik that I do not know, but I know overall because I believed this could have been part of this intervention platoon, and the overall commander was Miko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the commander of Kaonik had any authority over the intervention platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were questioned in this building. Do you perhaps recall, when you entered this building, could you smell food, whether food was prepared there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What were you questioned about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On all kinds of things. For instance, why was I at my brother's house; why was a certain person called Berber in this street; why a person -- I do not know if I should mention his name, but he was Croatian -- why was he spending so much time with us in the days leading to the conflict? They were asking me all kinds of things to which I had no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they ask anything about weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why not? They asked me for my personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What type of weapons are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a pistol called Skorpion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it an automatic pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they also asking for something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from me. They were asking me where the radio transmitter was. I had no idea that it existed, let alone that I possessed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the Marelja who beat you. What did he want from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, gold and money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he know that you were wealthy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had information from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But this was a generally known thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could not have been known to him because he was not a local. Somebody from the local people gave him this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were taken to Kula, did they also ask you for some valuables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the event that you describe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, we will not go back to that. Tell me, how did you know that you were going to be exchanged on 8th February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost all of us knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Red Cross, which had registered us and which visited again after that first registration visit, suggested that on this day, 8th February, would take place. But I learned about the exact date and time from the guards at Kula who came -- how shall I put it -- to give us the good news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, when did the Red Cross register you; do you recall that? Maybe you do not recall the date, but in relation to the time when you first arrived in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I think it was sometime around 1st February. I am sorry that I do not have the ID card here, because that is where -- it is written down there, but I think it was around February 1st or maybe 31st January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that one morning you were awakened by some big noise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, you described it, so I am not going to dwell on it. The military policemen arrived and arrested the people who had taken valuables from the people at Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military policemen intervened at the suggestion of the Kaonik camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The intervention came after somebody reported that there was somebody among the soldiers, the HVO soldiers up at Kula and so they thought the that somebody had overstepped the limits and they called the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We do seek a redaction at page 62, lines 12, 13 and 14. I believe it has already been shown to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Witness F, you have completed your testimony. The International Criminal Tribunal thanks you for having come and for your testimony. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. May it please the court. The next witness is asking for protective measures and the reason for his request has already been exposed to you by my colleagues, they did already explain to you in the course of this trial, why do they so often need and they feel they need protective measures. I am confident, therefore, that my learned friend, Mr. Mikulicic, Defence counsel, will not oppose this request, so I understand, and the court will decide accordingly and grant the measures, including face distortion and pseudonym for the witness, which I think will be letter G. We may introduce the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, have you any objections or comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objections, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Have you taken all the necessary protective measures, Mr. Dubuisson? Yes, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Are you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the declaration which the Registrar will give you. Will you, please, stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Solemn declaration: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. You are going to answer questions which the Prosecutor is going to put to you, please. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor. WITNESS G

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. The usher will show you now a sheet of paper on which your name is written. Please let us know and the court know, if that is your name, say "yes". If the contrary, say "no". Thank you. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Please show the Defence. (Handed). I tender the document as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, for this examination, you are Mr. G. Please do not refer to your name, to your real name, during this examination. Do you understand; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: The only personal datum we need to have from you is concerning your age. Which is your age now, today? How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And your faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Islam. I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Are you practising your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, if you do agree, I would like to bring your memory to January 1993, when you were living in Busovaca, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you living there with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How was the situation in Busovaca at that time in your neighbourhood, particularly from the point of view of ethnic interrelations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you think about my immediate neighbourhood, I had no problems with them, but generally speaking the situation of that period, there was some division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you be more detailed about that? Which kind of divisions were evident to you during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I repeat my question. You said that there were many distinctions between the situation in your neighbourhood and the distinction in the Busovaca area. Which kind of divisions were evident to you in that period of time in the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People -- people went to different groups. The Croats would be meeting more with Croats and the Bosniaks more with Bosniaks, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go to your neighbourhood, was it a mixed neighbourhood, were there Croats and Muslims living together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my street on the one side of the street were Muslims, that is Bosniaks and on the other side lived the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But was this intentional, was this because of the division, of the ethnic division you were referring to before, or just simply an accident, it happened to be so in the developing of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not intentional, it was -- for the most part, these were new houses, people lived there for up to five or to ten years and I built my house in 1985 and to the right the Croats lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Among your Croat neighbours was there Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you meet him on a daily basis, did you have any relation? Were you friends or familiar together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him, but we did not have common friends or did he socialise? We would just say "hello" if we saw each other in the streets but we were not really friends, close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: But did you have any one particular official contact with Kordic before or after your detention in Kaonik? Do you remember this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before my detention, I did not have any contact with him. Absolutely none. Afterwards I did, when I came out of the camp I did and the reason was it was Bajram and we in Busovaca could not go to the mosque. As we were neighbours, I went to ask for permission to go to Zenica to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, you mean that Muslims at that time were not allowed to go to the mosque, to attend their religious services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just then, when we had Bajram, the Bajram holiday, we were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did not allow you to go, by which authority were you forbidden to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We simply did not have freedom of movement to be able to go there. I could not really tell you exactly such and such a person prohibited us from going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go now to January 23rd, 1993. Do you remember what happened to you that morning? Can you tell the court what happened to you that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in the morning the sirens were on in town, the sirens from the fire brigade centre. I think it was about 6.00 in the morning, I could not tell you exactly but roughly about that time. My house has a first floor level. I was upstairs. I came down to the living room with my wife. She prepared coffee for us. I did not have any particular suspicions, but I already noticed HVO soldiers moving along a side street. Shortly after that they came in front of my door and said that I should come with them. They were wearing camouflage, though some were also in black uniforms. Some of them even had helmets and they had automatic rifles on them. They took me from there to the police station and they brought there too some other Muslims. I cannot recall their names. There were about 10 of us. From there we were sent to the Kaonik prison, or rather we were transported in a van to the Kaonik prison. I was in the camp for 15/16 days --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to interrupt you. How long did you stay in the police station and when did you reach Kaonik on the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we stayed for about one hour in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then when did you arrive at Kaonik; the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, during that same day. Kaonik is close to the police station, maybe three kilometres. Three and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened on your arrival at Kaonik? How did the situation and the place look like to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew the place from before, because the Yugoslav People's Army had their barracks there. When we were brought there it was under the control of the HVO and they put us up there. In fact, all that day they kept bringing in more Muslims and Bosniaks. I was among the first to get there, so that I saw them bringing in more and more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So, when you did arrive at Kaonik, your group was the first one to be introduced in the camp, according to what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not exactly say that we were the first, but we were among the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you brought that very day? In what kind of facility were you detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was a large room and inside were cells. There were several cells and we were put in those cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Kaonik after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you detained always in the same cell or were you changed to other cells? If so, in the same building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the same building all the time, but in different cells, because I was taken to dig trenches and as the groups came back we were not necessarily returned to the same cell. We would be -- I would be in one cell one day and then in another, another, but I was not in the same cell all the time, that is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did you take your meals? In the same building, or were they taken into the cells? Was the food brought to you in the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While you were in the cells, we would go out into the corridor. There was quite a long corridor in front of the cells, going across the middle of the building, and we would eat on a table, on a long wooden table, so that we were mostly eating in the corridors. We did not eat in the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Had you other opportunities to move along the corridor or to see what was going on in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I could not move around, but if we asked -- I apologise -- to go to the toilet --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then you were allowed to go to the toilet? How many times a day were you allowed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Please, may I get the translation. Were you allowed to go to the toilet more than once in a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now you understand me; yes. Were you allowed to go to the toilet and, if so, how many times in a day? As soon as you asked, were you allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do the translators think we can go on?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. One microphone is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many times in a day were you allowed to go to the toilet, just once or how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes whenever we asked, they would let us go, but at other times they would not let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were there windows in the cell you were put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were not any windows except for a window above the door to the cell. But you could not see anything outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You mean that it was possible to see what is going on in the hallway, in the corridor, if not directly by standing on somebody else's shoulder, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if we were to climb on somebody's shoulders, but no-one dared do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was there a peeping hole in the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. A small hole, but I said we did not dare look because the guards were outside in the corridors, so we did not dare look through to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you ever see or hear during your stay at Kaonik something unusual happening in the hallway, in the corridor, in the cells near were you were being detained? Beatings, screams, other unusual events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander or the warden, let us say, of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know his name but at the time when I went to the camp, I did not know him at all. Nor had I heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was his office in the same building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance to the building, on the left-hand side, there were two offices, where I saw guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now, I am going to show you a photograph. May I introduce this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you show it to Mr. Mikulicic, please? (Handed). Witness G, do you recognise the hallway of the building you have been detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you identify the places where you were taken when you were taking your meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can see a big stove made from a barrel and then this table over here that you can see, there was a long table there. That is where we ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle round it with the pen and sign it and mark it with the letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please point on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you, please, look at the photograph on that ELMO there? Show, please, again where the table was around which you usually take your meals. Can you draw a circle around it and sign it with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you point to the windows from the cells that look on the hallway, the windows over the doors of the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And, can you, please, now point to the direction which the warden's office was, if it is not in the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you draw an arrow in that direction, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). This was the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were the two offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The offices -- in this direction, the office was here, to this side and this side. (Indicating). If this is the door, that would be the entrance to the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you mark the door, giving entrance to the office with the letter "B", with an arrow and a letter "B".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender the photograph into evidence, please. Now, Witness G, during your stay in Kaonik, were you taken out of the camp, and for which purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I went to dig trenches and canals and dug-outs and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many times did you go trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many of them were taken together? How many prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went in groups of 20 to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And how were prisoners selected for this purpose? Were they called out at random or did the guards have a list of names for each day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not at random, they had a precise list of names for each group, where they were going to. We did not always go to the same place, we went to several places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did actually call out the names of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A person was designated in the camp. It was always one and the same person who called out the names for trench digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You do not know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did he get a daily list from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see because I was in the cell. My assumption was that he got the list in that office but I really do not know because I was in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where have you been taken trench digging during those days? Can you list the places and, please, can you sign them on the map that will be shown to you? It is a map that has already been produced into evidence. Here is a map for the judges and for the witness. Show it, please, to Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness G, can you show us the places where you have been taken trench digging and, as I have asked you to do before, circle them with a pen and mark with letters. If you tell us the places in order, according to your memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to several places, so I will mark those places where I went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Please do, and give us the names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bare; Prosje; Kula. (Witness marked map). Those are mostly the places I went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you, please, sign the names with letters, "A", "B" and "C"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bare, "A". Within the circle or outside it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: It does not matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that. Witness G, while digging -- and you said you have been taken there many times -- did you ever find yourself under fire or were you exposed to shooting by any of the opposing lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How did it happen? Do you have any specific memory as to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, when they would take us to the line for trench digging, they would simply tell us that we had to dig and they did not care that we were exposed to the possibility of being fired at. We simply had to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And was somebody of your fellows wounded or killed during this work and in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my presence, no. But I know that two people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And, therefore, how long approximately were you forced to dig during a single day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That differed. Sometimes we would dig from 7.00/8.00 in the morning until the evening. Sometimes we would dig day and night, and sometimes dig all day, all night and the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What about food, did you have a possibility to have some rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what do you mean "rest"? There was no rest. We were forced to dig. As for food, it was very poor, very, very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which kind of food did you receive and which quantities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall we say if we were digging all day, all the time, then another evening, then we would share a tin of fish food for two people. The HVO soldiers would just say that they did not get any food for us, so they would not give us any. When I said that the two of us would get one of these fish cans or some meat paste, that was to be shared between the two of us for the whole day. We would get food just once a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: From this, did any mistreatment or abuse take place on these occasions during work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank God I was lucky enough that in my vicinity there was no mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp sometimes some HVO soldiers would come but I did not know them. They were not from Busovaca. I know that they usually asked people to take off their watches and rings, if they had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were you forced to give some of your property, valuables, money, rings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I did not have any, but I was referring to others, those who had watches or money or gold, they were asked to turn them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Asked by whom, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my knowledge and from conversations I had later, there was an HVO soldier from Novi Travnik. They called him Marelja. I am not sure if that was his name or last name but I know he was called Marelja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then what was this soldier supposed to do seeing the prisoners, asking them to give him money, searching them and asking them to give properties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taking it for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Witness G, how did you leave the camp? Were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was exchanged. They said the conditions were such that those who wanted to go back to Busovaca could go and those who wanted to go to Zenica they could go there, or to go to Kacuni, which is near Busovaca. Because my family was in Busovaca I did not want to get separated from them. I then returned to Busovaca, even though they did not give us any guarantees after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So where did you choose to go first after you had been released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: In Busovaca, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Busovaca, that is right. In Busovaca that is where I went. For a while I was there at the my house and then later I moved to my mother's house together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Why did you move to your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As Croats were coming from other places, the HVO police would move them into these different houses and they simply told us to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And you did, in fact, leave all your belongings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then I gave it over to the Croats, whom I barely knew, but the HVO police kicked them out as well and brought in another two families so, of course, everything remained behind, the house, the belongings, furniture, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened then? Where did you decide to move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved to my mother's, so I stayed with her for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a while I requested to be transferred to Zenica and I went to the HVO office and I asked them to give me permission to leave. Then they set conditions for me of how I could leave. They said that my family had to stay behind and I had to send a doctor from Zenica to Busovaca and for each member of my family I had to bring over two Croats. They put down the name on a piece of paper. They asked for Dr. Barac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How many members were in your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we were seven, but my sister has since died, so for the seven of us I needed to find 14 Croats to be sent to Busovaca so they would be released. When I came to Zenica I could not find enough Croats who wanted to go to Busovaca --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, so actually your family was forced to stay, was not allowed to leave Busovaca; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I said that I was blackmailed that my family had to -- my family plus my mother, plus my late sister and her daughter, they all had to stay behind in Busovaca so that I could send the doctor and the group of Croats over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you went to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Zenica and I reported there. Then I went the to this doctor. I asked him whether he wanted to go to Busovaca and he refused right away. He did not even want to discuss going back to Busovaca. Then I asked him to give me a document stating in writing that this was his wish so I would not have any problems over it. Then I was told that there was a family who wanted to go, a family, there were five. In fact, there were four of them in that family and they also brought an acquaintance with them and I did not manage to find more of them there, so it took about 10 days and it was -- there was a lot of uncertainty. I had big problems trying to find people who wanted to go to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Finally, did they go to Busovaca, these Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Busovaca and after that my family was released from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long after these Croats reached Busovaca was your family released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they spent one night together there in Busovaca and then the following morning my family was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. G, I am Mr. Mikulicic, the Defence counsel for the accused in this case. I will ask you several questions and I would kindly ask you to respond to the best of your memory. Mr. G, you said that on that morning in January 1993 you heard a siren from the fire-fighting hall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who does give this signal, this siren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know in regular conditions, but when it happened I did not know who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Kaonik, did anybody receive you? Did anybody take down your data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I believed they did, but I am not sure of it. I think that they did because they had a list from which they were calling us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. G, when you were taken from Kaonik to the locations which are shown on the map, who guarded you while you were doing forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers, and they also had the letter "U", I should add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these the same people who guarded you at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not. No, they were not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know the guards from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know them because from what I could see, for the most part they were unknown to me and I do not know their names at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. G, you mentioned a person who asked for money and valuables from the people who were staying at Kaonik. You said that his name was Marelja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, this is how I heard him being called. I do not know whether this is his name or his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was this person, in what capacity was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. He simply would come into the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the cells have locks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean classic type of lock? Or you mean you have a sliding bar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No. But was there a key?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. G, when you came to Kaonik, did you have an opportunity to have religious rights observed? Did anybody prevent you from doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first and the second day -- the first two or three days, we did, but after that we went digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I did not understand, did you or did you not perform your religious rights, I did not understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did. Nobody prevented us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. G, you stated that two persons died when digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know both of them, but I cannot recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know under what circumstances they were killed, what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it did not happen in my presence, or in my vicinity, so I cannot say how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. G, you said that after your release from Kaonik, you returned to Busovaca to your family. How long after that were you in Busovaca; that is, until when were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until September. I think it was in September when I left Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means -- sorry, go ahead, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact month, I think it was in August or September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you said "released", do you mean when you left Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I left Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that means that you actually were in Busovaca in April when the second conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When this second conflict broke out, were you by any chance called to perform some duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what sense? In what sense "duties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you called to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we were taken to dig and they told us that we were civilian protection; we were no civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who assigned you to the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian protection that was with the HVO in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did someone else -- was someone else also assigned to the civilian protection among you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not just anyone, but most people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are talking about persons now that were not at Kaonik; is that correct? You understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not at Kaonik at the time. I had to come back from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is right. You were at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In other words, when I was in Kaonik, when I was released from the Kaonik camp, when I was in Busovaca, maybe I was not digging for 15 or 20 days. After that, they started forcing us to dig again all around Busovaca, not just me but everyone else who had come back to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Witness G, in examination-in-chief, you said after you were discharged from Kaonik camp the Muslims had difficulty attending the mosque for Bajram; what festival is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a Muslim holiday. It is a Muslim religious holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We have no more questions for you, sir. Therefore, you have completed your testimony. We wish to thank you very much for coming. Could the usher pull down the curtains, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that it is now time for the break until 4.10 pm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Prosecution witness is witness number 4 on the list of inventory of witnesses filed on 23rd February. In respect of this witness, too, your Honours, I am making an application on behalf of the witness for protective measures because, your Honours, I am seeking that pseudonym be assigned to that witness and also that he be granted distortion of his face during the course of his testimony. I believe Mr. Mikulicic has no objection to my application. He has been informed of this request and I believe he has no objection to this application, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, please, have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You are going to read the statement that the Registrar is going to give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going to answer the questions from Mr. Meddegoda, the Prosecutor. WITNESS H

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness will be known as "witness H". Witness H, I tender this sheet of paper to you on which a name is written and I ask you to read -- to look at the sheet of paper and confirm whether the name that appears on it is your name or not. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I tender that. Mr. Mikulicic may be shown that piece of paper and I tender that as an exhibit under seal, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, I take you back to the events in Busovaca in December of 1992 and January of 1993. Do you recall the tension that prevailed in the area during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you describe to this court what kind of tension was prevalent during the period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the HVO forces were armed, while the Muslim population was almost without any weapons. So, the tensions rose during that period. They had sort of a command of sorts over us. They had the control over the entire village, not just my village, but the neighbouring village as well. We were, so to speak, surrounded. So, there was a high degree of tension and we did not know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you are a Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And also your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, as far as your village is concerned -- I do not want you to name the village from which you come -- as far as your village is concerned, could you please tell this court the kind of tension that prevailed in your village in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when the conflict broke out, I was going to go and pick up my salary from the company where I worked, but I heard explosions. The tension was very high. We had very little weapons and so we did not have much of a chance to offer any resistance. We knew what was ahead. So a certain Mario showed up. I cannot recall his last name. He came and he said that we should surrender all the weapons, all the personal weapons, that it should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said a certain Mario turned up; did he turn up alone or did he show up with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time he came alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And do you know who this Mario is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lived, his house was just below my village. That is, his house was in the direction of the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was he a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A soldier. He also had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On the occasion when he came there, was he -- what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform. He had a few rocket-propelled grenades and he had an ammunition kit and he had an automatic rifle and I think it was a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did he come to your village a second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the meeting at which we were to decide whether to surrender our weapons or not. We told him that he could come again and that he would receive the specific answer then. After the meeting, we collected about two or three rifles, some ammunition and I remember one rocket-propelled grenade was put down on the pavement of this road. That was after we decided to turn in weapons. After that I left and I went home, so I do not know when and where these weapons were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, when Mario, the HVO soldier, came for the first time, did he ask the villagers to turn over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were the other soldiers at or near the village when Mario came to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the village was surrounded and, in the village itself, at the beginning of the conflict there was a lot of soldiers, so that when I started to go home, I saw about 30 of them at an intersection. I noticed three of them had the HV insignia on them while the regular soldiers wore the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be shown exhibit number 17? (Handed). Witness, could you please look at the exhibit on the projector and say to this court what insignia the soldiers were wearing on the occasion you saw this group at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local soldiers had the HVO insignia on, as I said, and it is this badge. (Indicating). The HVO insignia, as the locals called them, from Herzegovina, was this insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said some soldiers were HV insignia, now, which insignia is that, is it the insignia which is marked number 2 on the top left-hand corner of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the HVO insignia and that was what the local military were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Three soldiers, who were wearing a different insignia -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That insignia was the one that has "number 1" on the top left-hand side of exhibit number 17 which is on the projector now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, the villagers -- did you have a weapon with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a combined piece of weaponry. It was home-made and I did not surrender it, either. And it was also using the hunting rifle type of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were there others who did not surrender weapons from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only me and Jasmin Osmancevic, who had an automatic rifle, who was issued it in Zenica in the Public Security Service Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Why did he and you decide not to turn over your weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not believe in the safety that they had promised us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you say "they", who do you mean by the word "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it was the HVO soldiers and we could not believe them. It was later proven correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you went home after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, I take you back to April 1993. Most specifically, 15th April 1993; do you recall this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On that day, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the neighbouring village on business and I spent a little time there. I went to see a colleague of mine and we watched television and we saw on television the disappearance of Totic. I personally did not know him, but apparently he was some sort of a commander. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got there I just had enough time to have a coffee, when somebody knocked on the door, my sister went out and told me that I had to go outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you go outside when your sister asked you to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went out and I saw five soldiers; three of them had a sock on their heads with the eyes and nose cut out, so I could not recognise them. However, two of them I knew personally, somebody called Predrag, who was an active duty policeman in peace time in Busovaca and Pero. I am not sure whether it was Susnjar or Plavsic, I do not recall exactly his surname, he was a local man from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What were they dressed in when they were at your door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when you went out to talk to them, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They held their guns at the ready and they said that we were going for an interview with Andrijasevic Ivica, who was the commander of the Croatian army in my village. I knew where they were taking me. I did not really believe them that we were going for an interview. We started off and reached a neighbouring house, where they picked up another two and let me not forget to mention my brother, they picked up my brother as well. Then they searched the other houses but they did not find the others because I know where they were in hiding. They boarded us on to a minibus, as I call it, a combi, a van, and they transferred us to the former JNA barracks at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What time was it when you reached the former JNA barracks at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 7.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened upon reaching the former JNA barracks at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we entered the compound itself, we went to a hangar which must have been a warehouse, an ammunition depot of the former JNA. We got inside and someone called Anto Cakic told us to line up against the wall with our hands up and our fingers spread wide leaning against the wall and to stand there like that. They searched us, probably looking for weapons, but nobody had any. Afterwards they were looking for documents, any kind of insignia that people had, any marks or patches or stamps of the army, which had to be surrendered. The majority did what they were told. Some did not. When Anto Cakic said that they would search again and if they found anything at all linked to the army, that they would kill them on the spot. I saw some people actually eating up their military ID cards out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have any identification papers with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have anything on me, except for a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After that, could you say to this court what happened to you who were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That same night, about 1.00 am, drivers who used to drive humanitarian aid to Tesanj and Zavidovici and those areas south of Zenica. I do not know exactly all the places they went to, there were seven of them who were temporarily working in Switzerland and who had come on holiday. An enormous amount of money was seized from them later when my watch was taken as well. The next day, the local people from the neighbouring village were brought in. We were allowed to catch a breath of fresh air in front of the hangar. There were five or six guards there, whom I did not know at the time, but they could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you were brought to the hangar, and when -- when you were in the hangar and when the villagers -- the other villagers were a neighbouring village were brought to the hangar, did you see anything specific happen inside the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar, that morning nothing was happening because, as I said, we were outside, we were taken outside. But I could see when a car arrived, I could not see what make it was, they took us inside immediately. They told us to go into the hangar. That was when I saw Dario Kordic arrive because I knew him personally. He used to work in the same company that I worked for. Whenever people came, we were taken back inside. Probably so as not to see who they were and why they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The night you were brought into the camp, did you see who -- was there occasion to see the warden of the camp or the head of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He introduced himself as Zlatko Aleksovski, who said that he was the director of the prison, though I do not think that he can be the director in a prison. He could be that if it was a civilian prison but this was a military prison and a concentration camp. Therefore, for me he was a commander of all the military that were within the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was he wearing on the occasion you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes but sometimes he also wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That night when you saw him, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said there were villagers brought and you and the other detainees were taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I just said, we were just outside. Afterwards we were taken back inside the hangar. After that, most probably a commander from the Bare locality arrived asking for a number of men to dig trenches and canals. He selected about 30 people. They loaded us on to a large truck, make rubber, without a canvas cover, without seats and we were driven to this location at Bare in front of the elementary school there, the primary school. There were -- we were given a piece -- a loaf of bread to four of us and about 400 grammes of salami. Then we were taken to the spot where we were told we would be digging. About halfway there, the shooting started. We started to run for shelter but they prevented us. They said: "Do not run, because your people will not kill you", but it was not our people who were shooting. When we reached the place where the shooting was coming from, there was a large group of their soldiers there under arms and with HVO insignia. At that time, Zlatagic Ramo was wounded, Sunularpasic -- Ramo was hit in the neck and Salih was grazed near the head. They said that they would transport them to the Croatian hospital at Nova Bila. We went back to the school, then a civilian vehicle, I think it was a Golf, I do not remember exactly, I know it was a small vehicle, they took them away and from then on we left all trace of them. As I have just said, on the spot where the soldiers were, from where they shot at us, we were moved from that spot to a location in the direction of Kovacevac, where we were supposed to dig trenches, so that I knew where the fire came from and I knew from personal experience where the firing came because they were firing directly into our faces. When we reached that spot, we turned right towards Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, before you described what happened in Kovacevac, could you tell me after the meal you had with bread, you said there was a shooting. Now, you were being taken to the spot where you had to dig trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you taken to that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had their guns on the ready, there were three or four soldiers and they took us to the spot where we had to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you were taken by foot to that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were transported by car as far as the school, and from the school we went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, how far had you and the group gone when the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how many metres it was, but I know we came to a kind of plateau, an open space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said to this court that two persons sustained injuries as a result of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you know who fired at the group of detainees who were taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: From which direction did the fire come on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, it came from the direction in which we were heading. When we came to the place from where the fire had come, I said that we saw this group of soldiers. 15 or 20 of their HVO soldiers were there. Then cursing and insults started and from there we were taken off towards the village of Kovacevac, that is from the place where we came across the soldiers to the right. If it had been our people who had fired, then the people who had been wounded would have been hit on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who do you mean by "our people who had fired"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I am of Muslim religion, it was the army. Even though there were some Croats in the army but I am referring to the army, the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened at Kovacevac village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug there, we were digging trenches and canals there. After a time, we were transferred to another location, just below the village of Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig in Kovacevac village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: From there, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us just below the village of Rovna where I was told to dig a dug-out. That is when I saw a soldier with an HV patch. He was wearing a camouflage uniform and was armed with an automatic rifle. While digging, when I asked for water, he hit me with his rifle butt and told me to go on digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said the soldier was wearing an HV patch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If you look at exhibit number 17, which is still on the projector, which patch was that soldier wearing at the time you asked for water and he kicked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the emblem under "number 1".

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you asked for water, the soldier who was wearing this patch hit you with the rifle and ordered you to continue digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed until about 9.00/9.30 in the evening. Then we were taken back to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How were you taken back to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On foot, as far as the school at Bare. Then from Bare in the same vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, there were other occasions on which you were taken out of the camp for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I could list those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were those places you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kula, Podjele, Carica, Loncari, Kuber, which is just above the village of Jelinak. Once we also went to a location called Ravan, where we dug graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have your permission to show to the witness an excerpt of Exhibit 4? There are copies for your Honours, for the court and also for Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed). Could you please place that map on the projector, usher? Witness, there is a map on the projector. Could you please look at that map and, using a highlighter, circle on that map the places where you were taken to for trench digging and also the place where you were taken to dig graves. When marking, could you please say which place you are marking and could you circle that place and also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Carica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you place the letter "A" outside that circle, witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map) Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you place the letter "B" outside the circle. In Carica, what did you have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were digging also trenches and dug-outs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And in Ravan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, we dug graves there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you mark that with a "C"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you circle that area and mark it with the letter "D"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That could be circled and marked with the letter "E", witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Podjele.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could that be marked "F"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That will be marked with the letter "G".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). This is the area of Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you circle that area and mark it with the letter "H"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, after you came back from trench digging in Kula, which building in the camp were you brought back to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought back to cells below the hangar. Actually, this was probably another hangar, but it was adapted into cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall which cell you were put into after you were brought back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, cell number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I have your Honours' permission to show the witness an aerial photograph of the camp? It has already been tendered into evidence, your Honours. There are copies for your Honours and a copy for Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed). Witness, could you look at the exhibit on the projector and say to which building you were first brought into when you arrived at the camp on the night of the 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the building. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That was the hangar building to which you were brought into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you, please, using the highlighter, could you circle that building and mark that building with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: A while ago you said that you were transferred to cell number 16 in another building. Could you recognise that building, the second building, on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Which building is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That one. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you please circle that building and mark it with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that into evidence, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness, in cell number 16, were there other prisoners detained as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were about nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you, please, describe to this court the size of the cell and the conditions within that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It measured somewhere 2 by 3. I do not know the exact measurements, we never measured it. I know it was small. Most of them were like that. The conditions were very poor. There was a hallway in the cell, itself that was very, very small. The cots were made wall to wall. It was all bunched together and some hay was thrown on top of it and that is where we slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you have heating inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in the cell. There was a stove of sorts in the hallway. Something that was nothing really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you have any electric light in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my cell, as well as all the other cells which were on my side, there was no lighting. The only light came from -- was coming through the opening which was barred. When the light was turned off, some light, some reflection would come to the cell number 16, but it was very dim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, going back to the hangar in which you were first detained, would you describe to this court the conditions in the hangar building, the building which you marked with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were also bad. When we first arrived it was just concrete floor.
